report.source_text: The CBCT revealed a round bony sequestrum at the area of the right upper first molar and almost complete radiopacification of the maxillary sinus (panoramic image of CBCT). The portrayed borders of the sinus floor were discontinuous, revealing a communication between the necrotic bone and the sinus cavity (cross-sectional image of CBCT) (Figure 2). The osteolysis extending beyond the alveolar crest of the maxilla was considered to be associated with the observed chronic sinusitis (almost complete opacification of sinus).

report.source_text: A surgical approach was implemented to remove the bony sequestrum. After raising a full-thickness mucoperiosteal flap a piece of devitalized bone, well-separated from the surrounding vital bone, was revealed. Following diligent curettage of the lesion, the bony defect and the sinus was irrigated with saline, and finally primary closure was achieved.

report.source_text: After 5 months, the patients remained free of symptoms and a second CBCT was carried through to examine the bone healing and the closure of the sinus. The CBCT showed regeneration of new bone at the site of the defect, restoration of the sinus floor and the remission of mucosal inflammation (Figure 4).

clinician.final_diagnosis: stage 0 medication related osteonecrosis of jaw diagnosis affecting the sinus (classification by American Association of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgeons [AAOMS])
clinician.trajectory_summary: A 62-year-old female with a history of osteoporosis treated with ibandronate for 4 years presented with pain, discomfort, and an oral fistula with exudate in the first quadrant, 4 months after an upper molar extraction. Initial periapical radiograph showed non-healed alveolar bone and a radiolucent process extending to the right sinus. CBCT confirmed a bony sequestrum, necrotic bone, almost complete radiopacification of the maxillary sinus, and communication between the necrotic bone and the sinus cavity, along with osteolysis associated with chronic sinusitis. No clinically exposed bone was reported. A surgical approach was undertaken to remove the bony sequestrum, followed by curettage, irrigation, and primary closure. Five months post-surgery, the patient was symptom-free, and a follow-up CBCT showed regeneration of new bone, restoration of the sinus floor, and remission of mucosal inflammation.

key_supporting_evidence.claim: Patient has a history of osteoporosis treated with ibandronate 150 mg once per month for four years.

Patient presented with nonspecific pain and discomfort at the first quadrant and an oral fistula with exudate upon pressure at the area of the first upper molar, without odontogenic cause, following an extraction 4 months prior.
Periapical radiograph showed non-healed alveolar bone and a radiolucent process extending to the floor of the right sinus.

CBCT revealed a round bony sequestrum at the area of the right upper first molar, almost complete radiopacification of the maxillary sinus, discontinuous borders of the sinus floor revealing communication between necrotic bone and the sinus cavity, and osteolysis associated with chronic sinusitis.
Surgical removal of the bony sequestrum was performed, followed by curettage, irrigation, and primary closure.
Five months post-surgery, the patient was symptom-free, and CBCT showed regeneration of new bone, restoration of the sinus floor, and remission of mucosal inflammation.
No clinically exposed bone was reported, supporting the 'stage 0' classification.

The initial clinical exam did not report clinically exposed necrotic bone, which is a defining characteristic of higher stages. The diagnosis of Stage 0 MRONJ is based on the absence of exposed bone despite symptoms and radiographic findings.
